Splashed-Ink Landscape

Sesshū Tōyō, 1495

Ink on paper, hanging scroll

Misty mountain landscape in splashed grey and black ink on pale paper.

Use this style

Sesshū Tōyō, Splashed-Ink Landscape, 1495. Tokyo National Museum. Source on Wikimedia Commons. Licence: Public domain.

About the painting

Sesshū Tōyō, a Zen monk and the most celebrated Japanese ink painter of his time, painted this landscape in 1495 for his pupil Josui Sōen as a sign that his training was complete. Above the picture, Sesshū wrote about his own studies in China, and six Zen monks added poems. It is a National Treasure of Japan, in the Tokyo National Museum.

The technique is haboku, splashed or broken ink. Mountains, trees and a village are suggested with a few quick, wet washes and dark accents of ink, and the empty paper becomes mist. The whole scene is built from what is left out.

How it looks on your photo

The only monochrome style here. Photos lose their colour and turn into soft grey and sepia washes with dark accents, like ink on old paper. It works well for landscapes, fog and architecture, and for portraits with a quiet mood.
